adds.title: Indiana bans driver's license gender changes despite public pushback
adds.summary: Indiana residents lost the option to change their gender marker on driver's licenses or other identification cards when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles' new ban took effect on Feb. 1, 2026, ending the long-standing route of obtaining such a change through a court-ordered gender change or physician statement. The ban culminates an administrative rule change the BMV initiated; LGBTQ advocates who testified warned it will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents. The article also reports that pending Indiana Senate Bill 182 would create legal definitions for sex and gender, ban amendments to birth certificates, restrict bathrooms in public schools and restrict housing in prisons. This is the state's 2026 identity-document law the record ties to Indiana's harshest-state rating.

adds.title: Indiana Senate backs bill restricting transgender school restroom use
adds.summary: On Jan. 27, 2026, Indiana Senate Republicans approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House; the bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on their reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. Author Sen. Liz Brown, R-Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women 'continue to have their private spaces'; opponents including GenderNexus argued that letting anyone 'directly or indirectly injured' sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement. This documents the escalating bathroom restrictions the record cites as a driver of Indiana's adult-risk rating.

adds.title: Indiana Supreme Court denies birth certificate gender change in split ruling
adds.summary: In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases of transgender girls seeking to change the gender on their birth certificates; the denials left appeals-court rulings standing that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One case involved a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access. This is the court outcome that kept Indiana's birth-certificate gender-marker change off limits ahead of the 2026 identity-document law.

adds.title: Utah joins 10 other states in regulating bathroom access for transgender people
adds.summary: On Jan. 30, 2024, Republican Gov. Spencer Cox signed HB 257, making Utah the latest state to regulate bathroom access for transgender people; the law requires people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings that match their sex assigned at birth. Under the legislation transgender people can defend themselves against complaints by showing documentation of gender-affirming care, and new government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. NBC reported at least 10 other states had passed similar bathroom-regulation laws by then and quoted the ACLU of Utah opposing the bill for risking discriminatory enforcement. This is the dated enactment of the adult-reaching bathroom ban the record attributes to HB 257.

adds.title: H.B. 257 Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities
adds.summary: Official Utah Legislature page for HB 257 ('Sex-based Designations for Privacy, Anti-bullying, and Women's Opportunities'): the bill's action history shows it was introduced Jan. 11, 2024, advanced through House and Senate committee and floor stages across several substitute versions, and the page's last recorded action is '30 Jan 2024, Governor Signed.' Subject tags cover state facilities, K-12 and higher education, and health and human services. Primary state-government confirmation of the bill number, short title and Jan. 30, 2024 signing date.

adds.title: Utah Creates 'Snitch Line' For Trans People In Bathrooms
adds.summary: Star Observer documents the reporting mechanism Utah set up under HB 257: a form through which residents can report transgender people in 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms, with complainants able to choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each 'violation'. The article says the form implements HB 257, 'Sex-Based Designations for Privacy, Anti-Bullying and Women's Opportunities', passed in January 2024, which banned trans Utahns from using bathrooms or competing in a sport that matches their gender identity. This confirms the complaint channel the record lists among Utah's facility-law provisions.

adds.title: HB 1522 - Overview | North Dakota Legislative Branch
adds.summary: North Dakota Legislative Branch overview of HB 1522 (2023): an act creating new sections of the North Dakota Century Code 'relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student,' with a penalty provision and an emergency clause. The page records the 2023 regular-session progression and the final disposition — governor signed, with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on May 9, 2023. This is North Dakota's enacted 2023 transgender-student statute, relevant to the record's account of state anti-trans legislation.

adds.title: Identity Document Laws and Policies - Movement Advancement Project
adds.summary: Movement Advancement Project's identity-document policy tracker states that North Dakota's 2023 law 'bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery', calling it a stricter, more explicit surgical requirement than in many other states, and marks North Dakota a 'negative law' state in its map. This supports the record's placement of North Dakota among states restricting birth-certificate gender-marker changes.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nevada - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's state page for Nevada records that the state's anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation and gender identity/expression, and that since 2016 Nevada Vital Records issues a corrected-gender birth certificate on two affidavits alone, with sex reassignment surgery not required and similar changes available for driver's licenses and state IDs; a May 2017 law (signed June 22, 2017) abolished the 1988 requirement that transgender people publish their names in newspapers before legal sex changes on government documents. In March 2018 the state's Medicaid agency announced it would cover sex-reassignment surgery costs, state law bans health insurers from discriminating against transgender patients, and Nevada offers an 'X' third-gender designation on driver's licenses, birth certificates and state IDs with no medical documentation required (2019). In May 2023 the governor signed a law protecting transgender and intersex individuals in state correctional facilities, while the legislature-passed 2023 omnibus bill SB 302 shielding gender-affirming care and abortion was vetoed by the governor; a separate June 2023 bill requiring health insurers, including Medicaid, to cover all medically necessary gender-affirming treatments became law effective January 1, 2024. In April 2025 the Nevada Interscholastic Activities Association reversed its 2016 policy and now requires transgender athletes to compete under their sex assigned at birth.

adds.title: Transgender rights in the United States - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The national-framework page that governs federal policy applying within Nevada: on January 20, 2025 President Trump signed Executive Order 14168 ('Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government'), redefining federal policy to recognise only two sexes based on gametes, revoking federal recognition of a third gender and directing agencies to implement the binary definition; on January 22, 2025 the State Department suspended applications for passport gender-marker changes, ending the 'X' passport option available on a self-identification basis from 2022 to 2025, while passports issued before January 2025 with markers not matching assigned sex remain valid. The page also records the June 18, 2025 US Supreme Court ruling in United States v. Skrmetti holding state bans on gender-affirming care for minors constitutional. This confirms the 2025 federal document and passport rollbacks the record says apply here as across the federation.

adds.title: LGBT rights in India - Wikipedia
adds.summary: The national-framework page under which a trans visitor in Punjab (India) stands: on September 6, 2018 the Supreme Court's five-judge bench ruled unanimously in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts and holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution, while preserving the provision for non-consensual acts; in July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omitted Section 377 entirely. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender, codified by the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, which the page says bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing. The page carries no Punjab-specific law or institution targeting trans people, consistent with the record's finding that the documented signal in Punjab is institutional rather than criminal.

adds.title: Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia on India's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019), the national statute governing transgender people in Punjab: it was passed by the Lok Sabha on August 5, 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on November 26, 2019, received presidential assent on December 5, 2019, and has been in force since January 10, 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA ruling, it grants transgender people the right to declare self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people, though the page records criticism that it omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On January 27, 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality. This protective national framework is the statute a trans visitor to Amritsar stands under and supports the record's statement that no statute in Punjab targets trans people.
